result.note: Tests the coal flexibilisation target (minimum load 55% to 40%) and the CEA cost comparison and solar curtailment mechanism; skips the Ember dollar estimate.

questions.prompt: In March 2026, India delayed by a year its plan to make coal-fired power plants ramp down when solar generation peaks. The plan requires retrofits so that these plants can cut their minimum operating level to which of the following?
questions.explain: The retrofits would cut coal plants' minimum use rate to 40% from the current 55%. The plan stalled because the federal regulator has yet to approve a framework on who pays for the retrofits.
questions.source: Coal plants need expensive retrofits to cut their minimum use rate to 40% from 55%, but no one has agreed on who pays.

questions.prompt: In March 2026, India postponed its plan for flexible operation of coal-fired power plants. Consider the following statements:
items: The Central Electricity Authority estimates that retrofitting coal plants for flexible operation is at least ten times cheaper per kilowatt-hour than battery storage.
When coal plants cannot ramp down, grid operators curtail solar output and compensate solar generators for the lost revenue.
questions.ask: Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
questions.explain: Both are correct. The CEA puts the retrofit cost at INR 0.28 to INR 0.60 per kilowatt-hour against INR 5.76 to INR 6.04 for battery storage, and the compensation paid to curtailed solar generators is funded through higher electricity tariffs.
questions.source: Retrofitting would add just INR 0.28 to INR 0.60 per kilowatt-hour to tariffs, versus INR 5.76 to INR 6.04 for battery storage, making flexible coal at least ten times cheaper, according to the Central Electricity Authority.
